gaps.sentence: The house ___ windows were broken has now been sold.
gaps.explanation: 'Whose windows' — the windows belong to the house.

gaps.sentence: The company's shares, ___ rose sharply yesterday, are still undervalued.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' refers to the shares; 'that' is impossible in a clause set off by commas.

gaps.sentence: He passed all his exams first time, ___ surprised everyone.
gaps.hint: refers to the whole previous clause
gaps.explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole idea ('he passed first time'); this non-defining use never takes 'that'.

gaps.sentence: Mount Everest, ___ was first climbed in 1953, attracts hundreds of climbers every year.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' introduces extra information about the mountain; 'that' is wrong after a comma.

gaps.sentence: This is the beach ___ we used to play as children.
gaps.explanation: 'Where' introduces place information; 'we used to play' already has a subject and object, so 'which' is impossible.

gaps.sentence: She was two hours late, ___ annoyed the interviewer.
gaps.hint: comment on the whole situation before the comma
gaps.explanation: When a clause comments on the whole previous statement, use 'which' after the comma.

gaps.sentence: The degree to ___ the climate is changing alarms scientists.
gaps.explanation: 'The degree to which ...' is a formal pattern used with abstract nouns; 'that' cannot follow the preposition.

gaps.sentence: They said nothing at all, ___ I found rather strange.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' here means 'and this'; it refers to the whole situation and follows a comma.
